a: Remove the cover, rotate the lock handle, the door falls inward, then egress on the descent devices.

q: B043 vs B044 flight plan?
a: B043 is the international fuel reserve, 8.3.2.3. B044 is planned redispatch.
qOrig: What is the difference between a BO44 vs B043 flight plan?
detail: B043 is the Ops Spec authorizing special fuel reserves in international operations, where the 10 percent applies only to planned oceanic/remote continental time and the final reserve is 45 minutes at normal cruise consumption. Ops Spec B044 is one of the authorizations cited for planned redispatch under FOM 8.5.9, where the flight is dispatched to an intermediate destination and redispatched enroute to the intended destination to minimize the 10 percent fuel requirement.
quote: "Ops Spec B043"
note: Both reduce carried fuel but by different mechanisms: B043 narrows the window the 10 percent applies to; redispatch (B044) shortens the leg the 10 percent is computed against. 8.5.9 lists Ops Specs A002, A004, A008, B044 and B050.

q: Standard release vs redispatch?
a: Redispatch runs two plans and meets the 10 percent reserve only to an intermediate destination, so you carry less fuel.
qOrig: Discuss the differences between a standard dispatch release vs a Re-Dispatch/Re-Release
detail: A standard release dispatches you to the destination on one plan. Planned redispatch is an FAA-authorized flag procedure that minimizes the fuel needed to meet the 10 percent requirement. You operate with two plans: the original dispatch to the intermediate destination, and a second plan from a planned redispatch waypoint to the intended destination. The terms of the original release govern until the Captain and Dispatcher concur on the redispatch, and once redispatched those terms are operative and cannot be changed except by Captain and Dispatcher concurrence.
quote: "The terms of original Dispatch Release must be adhered to until the Captain and the Dispatcher concur on the terms of the redispatch."
note: Terminology to have cold: Intended Destination is the ultimate destination from the redispatch waypoint; Intermediate Destination is the one on the original release; the Redispatch Point is the common point on both flight plans where the continue decision is made. Regulatory basis 14 CFR 121.631 plus Ops Specs A002/A004/A008/B044/B050. Procedures at 8.5.9.1.

secTitle: Know Weather Minima & Limitations for Dispatch, Takeoff, Approach, and Landing
q: Destination alternate weather required to depart?
a: At or above the derived alternate minimums for the ETA at the alternate.
qOrig: Weather required to be at our destination/destination alternate (Flag) to depart?
detail: A flight may not be dispatched unless the weather at the destination alternate is forecast at or above the alternate minimums for the time the aircraft would arrive there. Those minimums come from the Derived Alternate Airport IFR Weather Minimums table in 8.2.2.1 under Ops Spec C055. For a single straight-in non-precision approach the derivation is MDA(H) plus 400 ft and visibility plus 1 sm or 1600 m. Exemption 20108 allows dispatch with alternates not meeting this criteria under specific conditional-language limits.
ref: FOM 8.2.2.1 Destination Alternate Airport Weather Requirements
quote: "A flight may not be dispatched to the destination airport unless the weather conditions at a destination alternate airport are forecast to be at or above the alternate minimums"
note: Second alternate rules live in 8.2.2.2 and Exemption 20108 in 8.2.2.3. Rev 125.1 added a DOM 3.000 cross-reference and the Ops Spec A010(e) rule that a second alternate is required for flag or supplemental flights to an international airport with information missing from the METAR, and both destination alternates must have a complete METAR and TAF.

secTitle: Know Weather Minima & Limitations for Dispatch, Takeoff, Approach, and Landing
q: ETOPS alternate weather before departure?
a: Ops Spec C055 minima from earliest to latest landing time, field conditions allowing a safe landing.
qOrig: Weather required for ETOPS alternate airport(s) prior to departure?
detail: The Dispatcher will not list an airport as an ETOPS alternate unless reports or forecasts indicate weather will be at or above the ETOPS alternate minima in Ops Spec C055 (see 8.2.2) for the whole window it might be used, earliest to latest possible landing time, and field condition reports indicate a safe landing can be made. The earliest and latest arrival times are printed on the Dispatch Release, so if the flight is significantly delayed the crew should reassess whether those times still hold.
quote: "Field condition reports indicate that a safe landing can be made."
note: Each designated ETOPS alternate must have RFFS equivalent to ICAO Category 4 or higher, with a 30-minute response time, which means equipment available on arrival of the diverting airplane, not equipment parked there in advance. Rev 125 keyed the adequate airport and ETOPS alternate definitions to 8.1.3 Authorized Airports rather than Ops Spec B342/C070.

secTitle: Know Weather Minima & Limitations for Dispatch, Takeoff, Approach, and Landing
q: ETOPS alternate weather in flight?
a: Crew operating minima, less restrictive than dispatch planning. The rule changes at the EEP.
qOrig: Weather required for ETOPS alternate airport(s) in flight?
detail: From after takeoff until approaching the EEP, alternate weather must be at or above the crew's operating minima, that is what the operating crew needs to fly the approach given their minima and any applicable MEL, and the alternate must remain suitable to conduct an IAP. A turnback is required if an ETOPS alternate is no longer available. After the EEP a turnback is NOT required if the weather is below crew minima or the runway is unusable; instead you attempt to establish a new ETOPS alternate with Dispatch, which may lead to a turnback, reroute or continuation.
ref: FOM 6.3.5 In-Flight ETOPS Alternate Airport Weather Requirements
quote: "Note that these weather requirements are less restrictive than the criteria used by Dispatch in planning."
note: This is a favourite oral question because the answer changes at the EEP. If a METAR for an ETOPS alternate cannot be obtained after the EEP, a new ETOPS alternate must be designated. The FOM closes with joint PIC and Dispatcher judgment on the safest course of action.

secTitle: Know Weather Minima & Limitations for Dispatch, Takeoff, Approach, and Landing
q: Destination alternate weather in flight?
a: Crew operating minima, less restrictive than the dispatch planning criteria.
qOrig: Weather required at destination alternate airport in flight.
detail: Dispatch planning uses the derived alternate minimums table at 8.2.2.1. In flight the standard shifts to the crew's operating minima, meaning what the operating crew needs to conduct the approach given their minima and any applicable MEL. FOM 6.3.5 states plainly that the in-flight weather requirements are less restrictive than the criteria used by Dispatch in planning.
quote: "Note that these weather requirements are less restrictive than the criteria used by Dispatch in planning."
note: The dispatch-versus-inflight distinction is the whole question. Do not apply the 400-and-1 derived alternate minimums to an in-flight divert decision.

secTitle: Know Weather Minima & Limitations for Dispatch, Takeoff, Approach, and Landing
q: Takeoff weather minimums at the departure airport?
a: Takeoff minimums live in FOM 5.4.4 and 5.4.2.
qOrig: Weather required at departure airport for takeoff.
detail: Departure weather for takeoff is FOM 5.4.4 IFR Lower than Standard Takeoff Minimum Requirements, which for the 787 includes the sub-500 RVR case via the Takeoff Low Visibility Card in the PRC. A takeoff alternate is required per 5.4.2 when reported departure weather is below landing minimums for the runway of intended use.

secTitle: Know Weather Minima & Limitations for Dispatch, Takeoff, Approach, and Landing
q: Who can fly a low visibility takeoff?
a: Below 500 RVR use the Takeoff Low Visibility Card in the PRC. Foreign fields bind you to the higher of the 10-9A or OpSpecs.
qOrig: Any limitations on who can perform a low visibility takeoff?
detail: Ops Spec C078 authorizes lower than standard takeoff minimums wherever a procedure allows standard minimums. For the 787, takeoffs below 500 RVR (150 m) require the Takeoff Low Visibility Card in the PRC. At foreign airports published 10-9A minimums may not conform to Ops Specs, and crews are restricted to the higher of the 10-9A or Ops Specs. If takeoff minimums for a runway are NA, IFR departure is not permitted.
ref: FOM 5.4.4 IFR Lower than Standard Takeoff Minimum Requirements
quote: "(737/787) For takeoffs less than 500 RVR (150 m), see Takeoff Low Visibility Card in PRC."
note: NEW in Rev 125: 5.4.4 added 787 bannering and the HGS/HUD Takeoff Briefing Card, which is why this now applies to your fleet. The visibility table runs 5000/VIS 1 sm standard down through 1600, 1200 and 1000, with lighting and multi-RVR control requirements at each step. DESKTOP: the PRC card itself is not in this environment. Related: 5.3.11 Taxi Operations Low Visibility, and a takeoff alternate is required per 5.4.2 when departure weather is below landing minimums for the runway of intended use.

secTitle: Know Weather Minima & Limitations for Dispatch, Takeoff, Approach, and Landing
q: Visibility drops on approach. Can you continue?
a: Yes, if you already started the final approach segment. Continue to DA/DH or MDA.
qOrig: If the visibility drops while on the approach, can we continue the approach?
detail: Do not begin the final approach segment unless the latest reported RVR, visibility, or ceiling if required, is at or above the authorized minimums. However, if a weather report is obtained AFTER the final approach segment has been initiated and it indicates below minimum conditions, the pilot may continue the approach to DA/DH or MDA.
quote: "the pilot may continue the approach to DA/DH or MDA."
note: The trigger is the start of the FINAL APPROACH SEGMENT, not the FAF crossing or the clearance. For non-precision and CAT I: TDZ RVR is controlling, Mid and Rollout are advisory, and Mid may substitute if TDZ is unavailable. RVR above 6000 is advisory only. Visibility below 1/2 sm is not authorized and shall not be used for approach minimums.

secTitle: Know Weather Minima & Limitations for Dispatch, Takeoff, Approach, and Landing
q: Different visibility rules at international airports?
a: Yes. Some ICAO states allow Converted Meteorological Visibility when RVR is not reported.
qOrig: Are there different requirements at some international airports?
detail: Some ICAO countries allow use of Converted Meteorological Visibility (CMV) when RVR is not reported, for approaches that are not low-visibility. The FOM directs you to the Aerodrome Operating Minimums and Converted Meteorological Visibility references in the Jeppesen Publications for further guidance.
quote: "Some ICAO countries allow for use of Converted Meteorological Visibility (CMV) when RVR is not reported for non low-vis approaches."
note: Separately, at foreign airports the published 10-9A takeoff minimums may not conform to Ops Specs, and crews are restricted to the HIGHER of the 10-9A or Ops Specs (FOM 5.4.4). Theatre chapters 19 through 24 carry the country-specific items.

q: Who has operational control of a flight?
a: The PIC and the Aircraft Dispatcher, jointly.
qOrig: Who has operational control of a flight?
detail: The PIC and the Aircraft Dispatcher are jointly responsible for preflight planning, delay, and the Dispatch Release, and jointly determine the suitability of weather, field and traffic conditions, airway facilities, and the filed route. Neither can dispatch alone; both must agree.
quote: "jointly responsible for the preflight planning, delay, and Dispatch Release of a flight"
note: Regulatory basis 14 CFR 121.533/.535/.537/.551/.557/.627 and Ops Spec A008. Captain-side point: joint responsibility is not shared authority in flight. Once airborne the PIC retains final authority under 2.1.2.

q: What requires Dispatch notification in flight?
a: Any abnormality or irregularity, including the events in the Pilot Reports Quick Reference table.
qOrig: What items require Dispatch notification during a flight?
detail: Flights experiencing abnormalities or irregularities, including but not limited to those listed in 7.2.3 Pilot Reports Quick Reference, shall contact Dispatch and report the details. Notification is mandatory; the timing flexes to safety of flight. If time does not permit contact in flight, contact shall be made after gate arrival. The 7.2.3 table also marks which events additionally need a FODO debrief.
quote: "“Contact Dispatch” implies that while notification is mandatory, such communications should take place as safety of flight considerations permit."
note: Rev 125.1 revised 7.2.3 to state the table is not all-inclusive and that the Company may request safety reports for items not listed when additional information is needed. Separately 11.1.3 covers Cabin notification, and 11.2.11 gives the NTSB briefing format for the Flight Attendants.

secTitle: Perform ACARS and FMS Initialization and Verification
q: How do you know the nav database is current?
a: CDU IDENT page. Verify the ACTIVE date range.
qOrig: How can you tell if the Nav database is current?
detail: During Initial Data set on the preflight flow, on the CDU IDENT page you verify the MODEL is correct, verify the ENG RATING is correct, cycle the active NAV database to erase all previously pilot-entered data, and verify that the navigation database ACTIVE date range is current.
ref: FCOM NP.21.2 Preflight Procedure, Initial Data
quote: "Verify that the navigation database ACTIVE date range is current."
note: Note the order: cycling the active database first is what erases previously pilot-entered data, so it is a data-hygiene step as much as a currency check. The IDENT page also confirms MODEL and ENG RATING, which is a real trap on a mixed fleet.

secTitle: Perform ACARS and FMS Initialization and Verification
q: Can you change the nav database?
a: Yes. NAV DATA on the CDU, activate the other cycle, only when it is valid.
qOrig: Can you change the Nav database? How?
detail: The FMC carries two navigation database cycles, active and inactive. NAV DATA is selectable from the CDU and is where the database cycle is managed. The operational rule is that you only make a cycle active when its date range covers the flight, which is exactly what the IDENT page ACTIVE date range check confirms.
quote: "Select NAV DATA."
note: DESKTOP: the full switchover procedure and any company restriction on changing the database in flight should be confirmed in the FMS Pilot Guide and FCOM Chapter 11, which are not in this environment. Do not perform a cycle change with a flight plan loaded without verifying the effect on the active route.

secTitle: Perform ACARS and FMS Initialization and Verification
q: How do you know the AMM database is current?
a: 787 EFB and AMM currency. Verify on the aircraft.
qOrig: 787 – How can you tell the AMM database is current?
detail: AMM database currency is checked on the EFB. Distinct from the NAV database (FCOM NP.21.2 IDENT page) and the ECL AIRLINE DATABASE revision (FCOM NP.21.18). Verify the AMM check on the aircraft or in the EFB user guide.

secTitle: Perform ACARS and FMS Initialization and Verification
q: How do you verify the correct ECL is loaded?
a: RESETS page. The AIRLINE DATABASE revision must match the ECL revision on the QRH front page.
qOrig: 787 – How do you verify the correct ECL is loaded?
detail: During the preflight flow you push the CHECKLIST display switch, select RESETS, then Verify/Set AIRLINE DATABASE. Select the AIRLINE DATABASE that has a REVISION matching the ECL Revision listed on the front page of the current approved QRH, then select RESET ALL.
quote: "Select the AIRLINE DATABASE that has a REVISION that matches the “ECL Revision” listed on the front page of the current approved QRH."
note: The QRH is the authority here, not the airplane. If the airplane database revision does not match the QRH front page, the ECL is not the approved checklist. RESET ALL after setting it clears any prior crew state.

group: Load Closeout/TPR Update and review procedure
q: Who reads the closeout data?

q: What is the main concept of the TPC briefing?
a: Threats first and jointly, then the PF plan, then considerations. Interactive, not a recital.
qOrig: Discuss the main concept of the TPC briefing
detail: TPC replaces a read-the-plate monologue with a threat-led, interactive exchange. The PM opens by naming relevant threats, the PF adds any others, then the PF briefs the plan and the considerations. It should be interactive, concise and focused on the big picture, with management strategies discussed as threats surface.
quote: "The approach briefing should be interactive, concise, and focused on the big picture."
note: Captain-side: an interactive briefing is where you set flight-deck tone. If the FO never speaks during your brief, the T was skipped and you have lost the main safety value of the format.

q: Max taxi speed and braking technique?
a: Not more than 30 kts on straight smooth taxiways, about 10 kts in congested areas.
qOrig: Max Taxi Speed/s, and Braking technique?
detail: Speed shall be limited to not more than 30 kts, achieved only on straight, smooth taxiways, and approximately 10 kts in congested areas. While taxiing in the ramp or gate area, any congested area, where taxi instructions are complex, or during reduced visibility, the Flight Crew shall devote full attention to taxiing the aircraft.
quote: "Speed shall be limited to not more than 30 kts, achieved only on straight, smooth taxiways, and approximately 10 kts in congested areas."
note: Note shall, and note that 30 kts is conditional on straight and smooth, not a blanket allowance. When operationally feasible, single-engine taxi is the standard procedure for fuel efficiency. DESKTOP: carbon brake technique (one firm application rather than repeated light braking) is FCTM Ground Operations, not in this environment.

q: Why keep groundspeed in your scan?

qOrig: Emphasize importance of keeping groundspeed in scan

A FICON NOTAM is how the runway condition code and contaminant reach the crew. FOM 9.1 covers wet and contaminated runway operations, with 9.1.12.3 stating that for LDA less than 7000 ft you do not use WET data. Groundspeed in the taxi scan supports the 30 kt and 10 kt limits at FOM 5.3.3.

q: Can you depart at night with runway edge lights out?
a: Only with visibility at least 1/4 sm or RVR 1600, and FODO permission.
qOrig: Can we depart at night from a runway where the edge lights are inoperative?
detail: If ALL runway lights are inoperative, takeoff is not authorized during darkness unless both conditions are met: reported visibility greater than or equal to 1/4 sm or RVR 1600, and permission of the Flight Operations Duty Officer. If only a PORTION of the runway lights are inoperative, visibility is at least 1/4 sm or RVR 1600, and the remaining lights or runway markings give adequate visual reference to continuously identify the takeoff surface and maintain directional control throughout the takeoff run, takeoff may proceed.
quote: "Permission of the Flight Operations Duty Officer (FODO)"
note: Two different tests depending on all versus partial. The FODO call is only required for ALL lights inoperative. This is a Captain decision item that people commonly get wrong by assuming any light outage grounds the departure.

q: Wet vs contaminated runway?
a: Wet is a visible damp or water film with no depth criteria met. Contaminated is beyond that threshold.
qOrig: What is the difference between a wet vs contaminated runway?
detail: The FOM carries the operational consequence rather than a bare definition: for a Landing Distance Available of less than 7000 ft, do not use WET data. The wet versus contaminated distinction drives which performance table you are allowed to use, which is why the LDA threshold matters more on the line than the textbook definition.
quote: "For LDA less than 7000 ft, do not use WET data."
note: DESKTOP: the full wet/contaminated definitions and the RCAM/Runway Condition Code tables sit in FCTM and the TALPA material, which are not in this environment. Verify the definition wording there. Related: FOM 9.1.13 Degraded Braking uses the Can U StoP mnemonic.

q: Braking action report vs RCAM?
a: Runway condition reporting. FOM 9.1 and TALPA.
qOrig: What is the difference between a braking action report vs RCAM?
detail: A braking action report is a pilot or vehicle observation; the RCAM is the matrix that converts observed contaminant type and depth into a Runway Condition Code. A FICON NOTAM is how the runway condition code and contaminant reach the crew. FOM 9.1 covers wet and contaminated runway operations, with 9.1.12.3 stating that for LDA less than 7000 ft you do not use WET data. Groundspeed in the taxi scan supports the 30 kt and 10 kt limits at FOM 5.3.3.

q: What is a Runway Condition Code?
a: The TALPA number 0 through 6 describing surface condition, driving braking action and crosswind limits.
qOrig: What is a runway CC (Runway Condition Code)?
detail: The Runway Condition Code is the TALPA output used to assess a contaminated runway. On the 787 it drives the landing crosswind limitation directly: RwyCC 6 gives 40 kts, 5 (Good) 40, 4 (Good to Medium) 35, 3 (Medium) 25, 2 (Medium to Poor) 17, 1 (Poor) 15, and 0 (Nil) is no operation.
ref: FCOM L.10 Landing Crosswind Limitations TALPA
quote: "The crosswind limitation is determined by entering the table below with Runway Condition Code or Control/Braking Action."
note: A FICON NOTAM is how the runway condition code reaches you. Reduce the crosswind limit by 5 knots on wet or contaminated runways whenever asymmetric reverse thrust is used.

q: Max takeoff crosswind?
a: Read the takeoff table by CG column. Reduce the guideline 5 kts if thrust is above 40 percent N1 at brake release.
qOrig: Max takeoff crosswind limitations?
detail: Takeoff crosswind limits come from the FCOM L.10 takeoff table, entered using the columns labeled 25 percent MAC and 30 percent MAC, which is why the takeoff table is CG and weight sensitive while the landing TALPA table is not. Reduce all takeoff crosswind guidelines by 5 knots if thrust is above 40 percent N1 (GE engines) at brake release for the takeoff roll.
quote: "Reduce all takeoff crosswind guidelines by 5 knots if thrust is above 40% N1 (GE engines) at brake release for takeoff roll."
note: Demonstrated crosswinds are for certification only and do not represent operational limitations; the tables are the limits. Do not interchange the takeoff and landing tables, they serve different functions. DESKTOP: read the exact takeoff table values off the FCOM L.10 PDF rather than quoting from memory.

q: What is TALPA?
a: Takeoff and Landing Performance Assessment. It drives Runway Condition Codes and the 787 landing crosswind limit.
qOrig: (787) TALPA; What is TALPA?
detail: TALPA is the framework that translates reported runway surface condition into a Runway Condition Code and a braking action, which then drive performance and limits. On the 787 the LANDING crosswind limitation is determined by entering the TALPA table with Runway Condition Code or Control/Braking Action: RwyCC 6 is 40 kts, 5 (Good) 40, 4 (Good to Medium) 35, 3 (Medium) 25, 2 (Medium to Poor) 17, 1 (Poor) 15, and 0 (Nil) is no operation.
ref: FCOM L.10 Landing Crosswind Limitations TALPA
quote: "The crosswind limitation is determined by entering the table below with Runway Condition Code or Control/Braking Action."
note: Reduce the crosswind limitation by 5 knots on wet or contaminated runways whenever asymmetric reverse thrust is used. Winds are measured at 33 ft (10 m) tower height and apply to runways 148 ft (45 m) or greater in width. Landing on untreated ice or snow only when no melting is present. Sideslip-only (zero crab) landings are not recommended at the higher crosswinds.

q: What is NADP1?
a: The close-in noise abatement profile. Alaska normal takeoff procedures satisfy it.
qOrig: What is NADP1? Describe associated procedures
detail: NADP procedures are governed by Ops Spec C068. Specific requirements, including gradients and altitudes for configuration changes, may be defined in aircraft-specific manuals, the 10-7, or the Jeppesen Airway Manual Flight Procedures Noise Abatement Procedures. Crews must comply with published noise abatement procedures at noise-sensitive airports unless severe weather, traffic conflicts or other safety considerations require deviation, in which case the Captain must request an appropriate ATC clearance. Normal takeoff procedures satisfy either the close-in (NADP1) or distant (NADP2) profile requirements.

q: Where are the ETOPS verification flight procedures?
a: FOM 6.5.10 ETOPS Verification Flight.
qOrig: Where can the ETOPS verification flight procedures be found?
detail: FOM 6.5.10 carries the HA ETOPS Verification Flight procedure under 14 CFR 121.374. An EVF is a revenue or non-revenue flight during which the Flight Crew is asked to assist Maintenance to confirm an ETOPS Significant System is operating normally or that an ETOPS significant problem has been resolved. It may be conducted on a non-ETOPS flight or during an ETOPS revenue flight prior to the EEP. 6.5.9 is the parallel AS procedure.
quote: "An EVF may be conducted on a non-ETOPS flight or during an ETOPS revenue flight prior to the EEP."
note: You are on the HAL list, so 6.5.10 is your procedure, not the AS 6.5.9 version. Know which one applies before an oral.

q: Any Dispatch call required after takeoff, before the EEP?
a: Yes. Report component status between 30 and 60 minutes after takeoff and before the EEP.
qOrig: Is there a communication requirement to Dispatch between takeoff and prior to the EEP?
detail: Between 30 and 60 minutes after takeoff and prior to reaching the EEP, the Flight Crew will call or send an ACARS message to Dispatch to report the status of the affected component or system. This report AND the return acknowledgment from Dispatch must be complete before reaching the EEP.
quote: "This report and the return acknowledgment from Dispatch must be complete before reaching the EEP."
note: Two-way requirement. Your report alone is not enough; Dispatch's acknowledgment must also be received before the EEP.

q: Component fails before the EEP. Can you continue?
a: No. You cannot proceed beyond the EEP and must land for repairs.
qOrig: If the component being verified fails prior to EEP, can you continue?
detail: If the item being verified is not operating normally, the aircraft cannot proceed beyond the EEP and must land for repairs.
quote: "the aircraft cannot proceed beyond the EEP and must land for repairs."
note: Unambiguous. The verification failing before the EEP removes ETOPS entry as an option.

q: Component fails after the EEP. Can you continue?
a: The FOM does not bar it. The prohibition is written against proceeding beyond the EEP.
qOrig: If the component being verified fails after EEP entry, can you continue?
detail: FOM 6.5.10 states the aircraft cannot proceed BEYOND the EEP if the item is not operating normally. Once past the EEP the verification-flight restriction has already been satisfied or failed at that gate. A subsequent failure is handled as a normal in-flight system failure, using ETOPS contingency guidance at 6.4.4 and the PIC/Dispatcher judgment framework.
quote: "the aircraft cannot proceed beyond the EEP and must land for repairs."
note: INFERRED from the wording of the EEP gate, not an explicit post-EEP statement. Confirm with a check airman. Treat a post-EEP failure on its own merits under 6.4.4 In-Flight System Failures and the diversion logic in 6.4.1.

q: What is the APU verification procedure?
a: Cold soak the APU at least 2 hours at cruise, then start within 1 hour of top of descent, by one of three methods.
qOrig: What are the APU verification flight procedures?
detail: To complete the APU verification the Flight Crew must either remain outside ETOPS airspace; or on flights able to remain at cruising altitude two hours or more BEFORE entering ETOPS airspace, complete the verification before the ETOPS Entry Point; or on flights able to remain at cruising altitude two hours or more AFTER exiting ETOPS airspace, initiate the flight with the APU running, shut it down after exiting ETOPS airspace, allow at least a two-hour cold soak, and initiate the APU start within 1 hour of top of descent. If none of these conditions can be met, initiate the flight with the APU running and keep it running for the duration.
quote: "Initiate the APU start within 1 hour of top of descent."
note: The cold soak requires the APU shut down at least 2 hours at a normal ETOPS cruising altitude, ideally between FL270 and FL350. That altitude band is the point of the test: it proves a cold start at altitude.

q: How does APU verification differ from a single component EVF?
a: It is a scheduled cold-soak-then-start test with its own timing, not a 30 to 60 minute status report.
qOrig: How do those procedures differ from an ETOPS Verification (single component) flight?
detail: A single-component EVF is a monitor-and-report task: confirm the system works, report to Dispatch between 30 and 60 minutes after takeoff and before the EEP, and land if it is not normal. The APU verification is an active test requiring a minimum two-hour cold soak at altitude and a start within 1 hour of top of descent, and it is normally structured around staying clear of ETOPS airspace or completing it before entry or after exit.
ref: FOM 6.5.10 ETOPS Verification Flight (HA) and ETOPS APU Verification Flight
quote: "Allow the APU to cold soak for at least two hours."
note: If the APU verification is unsuccessful, the Dispatcher and PIC must confer to determine the best course of action, as ETOPS entry may not be possible. That is a joint decision, unlike the single-component case where the EEP rule is automatic.

ref: FOM 5.5.6.5 Enroute RVSM Altitude Monitoring Requirements
quote: "between FL290 and FL410, inclusive"
note: At initial level off, pilots shall verify all altimeters are set to 29.92 and crosscheck them. Use of the standby altimeter as a primary is PROHIBITED in RVSM airspace.

q: RVSM equipment requirements?
a: Both primary altimeters, one autopilot altitude-control system, and altitude alerting operating normally.
qOrig: Are there aircraft equipment requirements to operate in RVSM airspace?
detail: The following shall be operating normally prior to entry into RVSM airspace: both primary altimeters, one autopilot altitude-control system, and the Altitude Alerting System. The autopilot should be engaged during altitude capture and level cruise, except where circumstances such as the need to retrim or turbulence require disengagement. Report reaching assigned altitudes if not in radar contact.
quote: "Both primary altimeters"
note: Three items only. A common wrong answer adds transponder or TCAS to the list.

q: RVSM equipment fails in flight. What do you do?
a: Notify ATC and Dispatch and coordinate a prudent course of action.
qOrig: What are you expected to do if you have a failure of required equipment while in RVSM airspace?
detail: In the event of required RVSM equipment failure prior to or within RVSM airspace, notify ATC and Dispatch to coordinate a prudent course of action. ATC may not require any action; however, a reroute or diversion may be required.
quote: "ATC may not require any action; however, a reroute or diversion may be required."
note: Both ATC and Dispatch, not one or the other. The FOM deliberately leaves the outcome open rather than mandating an immediate descent out of RVSM.

q: Diverting without a clearance. What altitude do you plan?
a: RVSM and diversion altitude. FOM 5.5.6.
qOrig: When diverting to an alternate without a clearance, what altitude should you plan to be below when
detail: RVSM airspace is FL290 to FL410 inclusive. When diverting without a clearance, plan to be below RVSM airspace so you are not occupying a 1000 ft separated level without clearance. FOM 5.5.6.4 requires notifying ATC and Dispatch on required equipment failure to coordinate a prudent course of action.

q: How early do you log on to CPDLC leaving the contiguous 48?
a: CPDLC logon. FOM 5.2.15.
qOrig: When departing the 48 Contiguous states, to assist ATC, how many minutes prior to departure is an
detail: Verified this session: CONUS lower 48 logs on during preflight to KUSA; Alaska climbing through 10,000 to PAZA; American Samoa NZZO; Australia YBBB. Oceanic Control Areas use a time window prior to entry rather than an altitude, per the FIR/OCA Pilot Reference Card. The aircraft keying sequence is FCOM Chapter 5 and the FMS Pilot Guide.

q: Airborne CPDLC logon window before the FIR?
a: It varies. Oceanic Control Areas use a time window before entry, per the FIR/OCA Pilot Reference Card.
qOrig: Once airborne, what is the CPDLC logon time window prior to the FIR (“Flight Information Region”)? Is it
detail: If equipped with CPDLC, log on either on the ground during preflight or after takeoff above 10,000 ft MSL, or as required by the specific FIR/OCA Pilot Reference Card. Oceanic Control Areas typically have a TIME WINDOW prior to entry that defines the logon window, not a specific altitude. The logon location and address vary: CONUS lower 48 during preflight to KUSA; Alaska climbing through 10,000 to PAZA; American Samoa climbing through 10,000 to NZZO; Australia climbing through 10,000 to YBBB.
quote: "Oceanic Control Areas typically have a time window prior to entry that defines the logon window, not a specific altitude."
note: The direct answer to the second half is no, it is not the same for all FIRs. Use the FIR/OCA Pilot Reference Card. For KZAK Oakland the portal phase_flows page carries logon 45 to 15 minutes prior to entry and not below 10,000 ft.

q: How do you log on for a departure clearance? Enroute?
a: CPDLC logon. FOM 5.2.15.
qOrig: How, specifically in your aircraft, do you logon for a departure clearance? Enroute?
detail: Verified this session: CONUS lower 48 logs on during preflight to KUSA; Alaska climbing through 10,000 to PAZA; American Samoa NZZO; Australia YBBB. Oceanic Control Areas use a time window prior to entry rather than an altitude, per the FIR/OCA Pilot Reference Card. The aircraft keying sequence is FCOM Chapter 5 and the FMS Pilot Guide.

q: What can you request over CPDLC?
a: Forms and CPDLC menus. Comply365 and the aircraft.
qOrig: What types of requests can be made through CPDLC?
detail: AIREP completion and retention, CPDLC request types, and plot saving or submission are company workflow and aircraft menu content. FOM 5.7.3.15 requires the entire cleared route be loaded for ORCN segments but does not mandate saving plots after every flight. Verify in Comply365 and on the aircraft.

q: Two minutes before a waypoint, what do you do?
a: Confirm the upcoming waypoint and the next one agree with the flight plan and clearance.
qOrig: Approximately 2 minutes prior to reaching a waypoint, what crew actions are required?
detail: Approximately 2 minutes prior to reaching a waypoint, confirm that the upcoming waypoint and the subsequent waypoint (next plus one) agree with the Flight Plan and ATC clearance.
quote: "confirm that the upcoming waypoint and the subsequent waypoint (next + 1) agrees with the Flight Plan/ATC clearance."
note: The next-plus-one check is the whole point. Verifying only the active waypoint will not catch a gross navigation error that begins one leg downstream.

q: What gets checked on the flight plan after waypoint transition?
a: Record time and fuel, compare to estimates, note the difference, verify LNAV, slash the waypoint, report position if required.
qOrig: What items are required to be checked on the flight plan after waypoint transition?
detail: After waypoint transition: record the time and fuel remaining from the FMC on the Flight Plan/Dispatch Release or the ACARS HOWGOZIT/Flight Plan Review and compare with the estimates, recording the difference where plus is ahead or underburn and minus is behind or overburn. Verify LNAV (or the required mode) is displayed in the FMA and mark the waypoint with a slash. Transmit the position report to ATC if required.
quote: "Record the difference (+ is ahead/underburn and - is behind/overburn)."
note: Note the sign convention, it is a common oral trip-up. The slash mark is the physical evidence the check was actually done, which matters on a line check.

q: Where is fuel remaining recorded at waypoint transition?
a: The flight plan or dispatch release, or the ACARS HOWGOZIT.
qOrig: On which document is the fuel remaining (at waypoint transition) recorded?
detail: Time and fuel remaining from the FMC are recorded on the Flight Plan/Dispatch Release, or alternatively on the ACARS HOWGOZIT/Flight Plan Review, and compared against the estimates.
quote: "Record the time and fuel remaining from the FMC/FMS on the Flight Plan/Dispatch Release or the ACARS HOWGOZIT/Flight Plan Review"

q: Ten minutes after waypoint transition, what do you do?
a: Crosscheck navigational performance and course compliance, and correct any anomaly immediately.
qOrig: Approximately 10 minutes after waypoint transition, what crew actions are required?
detail: Approximately 10 minutes after waypoint passage, crosscheck navigational performance and course compliance. The FMC navigation crosscheck is: using the appropriate scale confirm the aircraft symbol is on the programmed route on the ND; check cross-track deviation; verify the TO waypoint is consistent with the current route clearance; verify flight guidance is in the appropriate mode to remain on intended track to the next waypoint; and investigate or correct any anomalies or unexpected deviations.
quote: "Take immediate corrective action for any anomalies or deviations."
note: Cross-reference 5.7.4.11 Position Doubtful if the crosscheck does not resolve. If you are on a weather deviation, the FOM requires this process to be completed immediately rather than waiting for the 10-minute point.

q: Why track fuel score?
a: Fuel score, tropopause and plotting. FOM 5.7.3 and Chapter 9.
qOrig: Why is keeping track of the actual fuel remaining vs planned fuel remaining (“FUEL SCORE”) important?
detail: Fuel score is the running actual versus planned comparison recorded at each waypoint transition per FOM 5.7.3.16, where plus is ahead or underburn and minus is behind or overburn. It is the early warning for a fuel problem. Tropopause level affects OPT and MAX altitude and marks the jet core; FOM Chapter 9 and the performance chapter cover it. Plot retention is FOM 5.7.3.15 plus company practice.

q: Which fuel figure goes on the release, tank total or PROG?
a: Load closeout, TPR and TLR. FOM 5.2 and fleet performance.
qOrig: (787) Which fuel remaining is noted on the dispatch release, the EICAS fuel panel (tank total) or the PROG
detail: Load closeout reading and verification, and the takeoff/landing performance products. Takeoff performance hierarchy is Final TPR, then Preliminary TPR, then TLR. Using a TLR for takeoff demands attention to the temperature and altimeter assumptions baked into it. FOM 5.2 covers closeout and weight and balance; the SABLE Load Sheet is the official FAA weight and balance record. Landing analysis designators and request methods are in the performance system documentation.

q: OPT vs MAX vs RECOMMENDED altitude?
a: OPT is fuel optimum, MAX is the highest with required buffet margin, RECOMMENDED accounts for route and conditions.
qOrig: What is the difference between OPT/Max/Recommended altitudes?
detail: These are FMC and dispatch planning constructs. OPT is the altitude giving the lowest fuel burn for the current weight and conditions; MAX is the performance ceiling with the required manoeuvre margin; the recommended altitude comes from the flight plan and factors winds, turbulence and the route. FOM 5.5.10 Cruise Altitudes carries the operational policy.

q: Why does the tropopause level matter for cruise?
a: Fuel score, tropopause and plotting. FOM 5.7.3 and Chapter 9.
qOrig: Why is it important to consider the level of the tropopause regarding your cruise altitude?
detail: Fuel score is the running actual versus planned comparison recorded at each waypoint transition per FOM 5.7.3.16, where plus is ahead or underburn and minus is behind or overburn. It is the early warning for a fuel problem. Tropopause level affects OPT and MAX altitude and marks the jet core; FOM Chapter 9 and the performance chapter cover it. Plot retention is FOM 5.7.3.15 plus company practice.

q: Is there a tropopause chart in the release package?
a: Yes, in the release package. FOM Chapter 8.
qOrig: Do we have a chart in our dispatch release package that shows the level(s) of the tropopause with
detail: Release package contents (the Lucky 7), preflight planning and international release sections, country-specific guidance and the tropopause chart are FOM Chapter 8 plus the physical release. Verified nearby: 8.5 Flight Information Documents and Redispatch, 8.5.5.4 Flight Plan Body Legend, 8.5.5.6 Flight Plan Descriptions, 8.5.7 Dispatch Release Sample (HA) and 8.5.7.1 International Dispatch Release Example and Legend, both UPDATED in Rev 125.1. Country guidance is in theater chapters 19 to 24.

q: What do you expect crossing the tropopause?
a: Tropopause effects. FOM Chapter 9 and performance.
qOrig: What can expect when cruising near, or crossing through, the tropopause?
detail: Crossing the tropopause changes the temperature lapse rate, which changes OPT and MAX altitude, true airspeed for a given Mach, and often marks the jet core with associated shear and turbulence. FOM Chapter 9 Weather and the performance chapter carry the operational treatment.

q: When is an electronic plot required?
a: An electronic plotting chart should be used on all ORCN segments.
qOrig: When and under what conditions are we required to do an electronic plot?
detail: An electronic plotting chart should be used on all Oceanic and Remote Continental Navigation segments. The Flight Crew should load the entire cleared route into the approved charting services app, such as FD Pro X, on the EFB.
quote: "An electronic plotting chart should be used on all ORCN segments."
note: Regulatory basis AC 91-70 and Ops Spec B036. Note the word is should, and the requirement is the ENTIRE cleared route, not just the oceanic portion.

q: How do you plot on the EFB?
a: Load the entire cleared route into the approved charting app, such as FD Pro X.
qOrig: How do you plot using the EFB?
detail: The Flight Crew should load the entire cleared route into the approved charting services app on the EFB. FD Pro X is the app named in the FOM.
quote: "load the entire cleared route into the approved charting services app (such as FD Pro X) on the EFB."
note: DESKTOP: the FD Pro X screen-by-screen plotting workflow is vendor documentation, not FOM content. Confirm with the FD Pro Pubs Quick Reference guide in Comply365.

q: Must you save or submit plots after every flight?
a: Forms and CPDLC menus. Comply365 and the aircraft.
qOrig: Are you required to save/submit your plots and route after every flight?
detail: AIREP completion and retention, CPDLC request types, and plot saving or submission are company workflow and aircraft menu content. FOM 5.7.3.15 requires the entire cleared route be loaded for ORCN segments but does not mandate saving plots after every flight. Verify in Comply365 and on the aircraft.

q: When is it prudent to screenshot your plotted route?
a: Fuel score, tropopause and plotting. FOM 5.7.3 and Chapter 9.
qOrig: When would it be prudent to save your plotted route (take screenshot postflight)?
detail: Fuel score is the running actual versus planned comparison recorded at each waypoint transition per FOM 5.7.3.16, where plus is ahead or underburn and minus is behind or overburn. It is the early warning for a fuel problem. Tropopause level affects OPT and MAX altitude and marks the jet core; FOM Chapter 9 and the performance chapter cover it. Plot retention is FOM 5.7.3.15 plus company practice.

q: What prompts a SATCOM call to Dispatch?
a: ACARS and SATCOM aircraft procedure. Demonstrate on the aircraft.
qOrig: What circumstance precipitates a SATCOM call to Dispatch?
detail: ACARS menu structure, function directory, SATCOM keying sequence, preprogrammed numbers and printer paper are aircraft and ACARS documentation, best demonstrated on the flight deck during OE. FOM 7.1.7 covers SATCOM policy and 7.1.12 Reports to Dispatch.

q: Who do you call on SATCOM for maintenance or a guest issue?
a: ACARS and SATCOM aircraft procedure. Demonstrate on the aircraft.
qOrig: When we make a SATCOM call for Maintenance or guest issue, who do we call?
detail: ACARS menu structure, function directory, SATCOM keying sequence, preprogrammed numbers and printer paper are aircraft and ACARS documentation, best demonstrated on the flight deck during OE. FOM 7.1.7 covers SATCOM policy and 7.1.12 Reports to Dispatch.

q: How do you make a SATCOM call?
a: ACARS and SATCOM aircraft procedure. Demonstrate on the aircraft.
qOrig: How do you make a SATCOM (specifically which buttons, and in what order, must be pressed in/on which
detail: ACARS menu structure, function directory, SATCOM keying sequence, preprogrammed numbers and printer paper are aircraft and ACARS documentation, best demonstrated on the flight deck during OE. FOM 7.1.7 covers SATCOM policy and 7.1.12 Reports to Dispatch.

q: Where are the preprogrammed phone numbers on the 787?
a: ACARS and SATCOM aircraft procedure. Demonstrate on the aircraft.
qOrig: In the ACARS/TCP (787) where can you find a list of telephone numbers that are preprogrammed to call?
detail: ACARS menu structure, function directory, SATCOM keying sequence, preprogrammed numbers and printer paper are aircraft and ACARS documentation, best demonstrated on the flight deck during OE. FOM 7.1.7 covers SATCOM policy and 7.1.12 Reports to Dispatch.

q: Total VHF and HF failure. Any other way to reach ATC?
a: Communication failure and HF requirements. FOM 5.7 and 7.1.
qOrig: If you have a total VHF/HF radio failure, is there another way to contact ATC?
detail: Alternate means of reaching ATC include SATCOM voice, CPDLC, and relay via another aircraft on 121.5 or 123.45. FOM 7.1.8 carries Long Range Communication System requirements, which governs whether oceanic entry is permitted with HF unserviceable. FOM 5.7.4.9 covers CPDLC and ADS-C failure and 5.7.4.10 total LRNS or MCDU failure. Verified nearby: under CPDLC you must still obtain a SELCAL check on HF before the initial Gateway Fix, and if SELCAL is inoperative one crew member must monitor HF continuously (5.7.3.18, new in Rev 125.1).

q: Where are the current Pacific HF frequencies?
a: HF practice and chart data. Verify at the source.
qOrig: Where can you find the most current (pacific) HF FREQUENCIES in use for your flight?
detail: Current Pacific HF frequency sets and the position-report template come from the Jeppesen enroute pages, ARINC and the PRC, not the FOM. The day/night frequency rule of thumb is operating practice. FOM 7.1.6 covers HF policy and 5.7.3.19 the non-CPDLC report content.

q: Rule of thumb for HF frequencies and the sun?
a: HF practice and chart data. Verify at the source.
qOrig: What is the rule of thumb with HF frequencies vs the Sun?
detail: Current Pacific HF frequency sets and the position-report template come from the Jeppesen enroute pages, ARINC and the PRC, not the FOM. The day/night frequency rule of thumb is operating practice. FOM 7.1.6 covers HF policy and 5.7.3.19 the non-CPDLC report content.

q: Where is the HF position report template?
a: HF practice and chart data. Verify at the source.
qOrig: Where can you find a ‘template’ to make an HF Radio Position report?
detail: Current Pacific HF frequency sets and the position-report template come from the Jeppesen enroute pages, ARINC and the PRC, not the FOM. The day/night frequency rule of thumb is operating practice. FOM 7.1.6 covers HF policy and 5.7.3.19 the non-CPDLC report content.

secTitle: Analyze Weather Conditions Using Weather Radar System
group: FOM and FCTM guidance on Weather avoidance
q: Where are the ICAO oceanic weather deviation procedures?
a: FOM 5.7.4.4 through 5.7.4.6, from ICAO Doc 4444.
qOrig: Where can you find the ICAO Weather Deviation procedures for Oceanic Controlled Airspace?
detail: Oceanic weather deviation procedures are at FOM 5.7.4.4 Weather Deviation Procedures for Oceanic Airspace, with 5.7.4.5 covering the case where controller-pilot communications are established and 5.7.4.6 covering when a revised clearance cannot be obtained, including the Weather Deviation Table. The regulatory source is ICAO Doc 4444.
ref: FOM 5.7.4.4 Weather Deviation Procedures for Oceanic Airspace
quote: "ICAO Doc 4444"
note: Sits inside 5.7.4 Special Procedures for In-Flight Contingencies, which also carries navigation systems failure (5.7.4.8), CPDLC/ADS-C failure (5.7.4.9), total LRNS or MCDU failure (5.7.4.10), Position Doubtful (5.7.4.11) and Gross Navigation Error (5.7.4.13).

secTitle: Analyze Weather Conditions Using Weather Radar System
group: FOM and FCTM guidance on Weather avoidance
q: How do you request a weather deviation?
a: Voice with WEATHER DEVIATION REQUIRED, or a CPDLC lateral downlink.
qOrig: How, specifically to your aircraft, do can you make a weather deviation request?
detail: Initiate communications with ATC via voice or CPDLC. A rapid response may be obtained by either stating WEATHER DEVIATION REQUIRED to indicate priority is desired, or requesting the deviation using a CPDLC lateral downlink message. Inform ATC when the deviation is no longer required or has been completed and you have returned to the cleared route.
ref: FOM 5.7.4.4 Weather Deviation Procedures for Oceanic Airspace
quote: "Requesting a weather deviation using a CPDLC lateral downlink message."
note: If it escalates, the urgency call is PAN-PAN spoken three times, or a CPDLC urgency downlink message.

secTitle: Analyze Weather Conditions Using Weather Radar System
group: FOM and FCTM guidance on Weather avoidance
q: How do you insert the offset in the CDU?
a: FMC and CDU procedure. FCOM and the FMS Pilot Guide.
qOrig: Once received, how (aircraft CDU/FMS specific) can you insert the offset distance?
detail: FMC and CDU manipulation: alternate navigation, destination change, offset entry, wind uplink, descent initiation, and autopilot requirements on RNAV procedures. FCOM Chapter 11 and the FMS Pilot Guide. Related FOM policy: 5.7.4.7 SLOP for offsets and 5.7.4.8 Navigation Systems Failure.

secTitle: Analyze Weather Conditions Using Weather Radar System
group: FOM and FCTM guidance on Weather avoidance
q: How far do you stand off severe cells?
a: The FOM publishes no standoff distance, only the deviation request and no-clearance procedure.
qOrig: How far (in nm’s) should you avoid Severe CB’s if possible? Which direction? Vertically?
detail: FOM 5.7.4.4 through 5.7.4.6 govern the oceanic deviation itself rather than a standoff radius. Say WEATHER DEVIATION REQUIRED for priority, or send a CPDLC lateral downlink. Inform ATC when the deviation is no longer required or is complete and you are back on the cleared route.
ref: FOM 5.7.4.4 Weather Deviation Procedures for Oceanic Airspace

secTitle: Analyze Weather Conditions Using Weather Radar System
group: FOM and FCTM guidance on Weather avoidance
q: No deviation clearance. What do you do?
a: Exercise emergency authority, broadcast PAN-PAN three times, deviate off the track system, and offset 300 ft if deviating 5 nm or more.
qOrig: If a weather deviation clearance cannot be attained, what is the procedure to deviate around weather?
detail: If you cannot continue per clearance due to dangerous weather and no prior clearance can be obtained, the Captain should exercise emergency authority and communicate the urgency signal PAN-PAN spoken three times, or a CPDLC urgency downlink, as early as possible. Until cleared: deviate away from an organized track or route system if possible; broadcast identification, flight level, position including route/track, and intentions at suitable intervals on the frequency in use and 121.5, with 123.45 as backup; watch for conflicting traffic visually and on TCAS; turn on all exterior lights. For deviations less than 5 nm maintain assigned flight level. For deviations of 5 nm or more, at approximately 5 nm from track initiate the prescribed altitude change.
ref: FOM 5.7.4.6 Revised ATC Clearance Cannot be Obtained
quote: "If possible, deviate away from an organized track or route system."
note: Weather Deviation Table 5.7.4.6(1). Flying EAST (000 to 179 magnetic): deviating LEFT descend 300 ft, RIGHT climb 300 ft. Flying WEST (180 to 359 magnetic): LEFT climb 300 ft, RIGHT descend 300 ft. Returning to track, be at assigned flight level within approximately 5 nm of centerline. If you are cleared a specific distance and then denied more, apply the altitude offset immediately.

secTitle: Analyze Weather Conditions Using Weather Radar System
group: FOM and FCTM guidance on Weather avoidance
q: What do you report to Dispatch when deviating?
a: The FOM requires reporting the deviation. No four-item list exists in Rev 125.1.
qOrig: What are the four items that are required to be reported to dispatch when deviating?
detail: FOM 5.7.4.4 requires informing ATC when a weather deviation is no longer required or has been completed and the aircraft has returned to the cleared route. For Dispatch, the holding report analogue at 5.5.15.1 requires fix, EFC and fuel on board, plus diversion plans if applicable.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
q: What drives normal fuel planning?
a: Wind and weather, traffic delays, MEL and CDL penalties, turbulence, altitude, one approach and a possible miss.
qOrig: What items must you keep in mind when doing fuel planning (normal flight)?
detail: Per 14 CFR 121.647 the following must be considered: wind, severe weather and other forecast weather conditions; anticipated traffic delays; MEL/CDL limitations and penalties; turbulence and cruise altitude; one instrument approach and possible missed approach at destination; and any other conditions that may delay landing.
quote: "One instrument approach and possible missed approach at destination"
note: Captain-side: if you and the Dispatcher cannot agree on extra fuel, the Captain has the final decision for fuel on board (8.3.1.2). Both parties must agree BEFORE fueling begins, and the crew should contact Dispatch at least 30 minutes prior to pushback with changes. No flight may begin takeoff roll with less than (HA) MIN TAKEOFF FUEL.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
q: Domestic dispatch fuel requirement?
a: Destination, most distant alternate, plus 45 minutes. With no alternate, destination plus 55 minutes.
qOrig: What are the dispatch fuel requirements for domestic operations?
detail: Flights must be dispatched with enough fuel to fly to the airport to which dispatched, and either fly to and land at the most distant alternate with enough fuel to fly 45 minutes at last cruise altitude consumption rate, or with no alternate required, fly for 55 minutes at last cruise altitude consumption rate.
quote: "With no alternate, fly for 55 minutes at last cruise altitude consumption rate."
note: 14 CFR 121.639. Both reserves are at LAST CRUISE ALTITUDE consumption rate, not holding. Applicable areas at 8.1.1.1.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
q: Flag dispatch fuel requirement?
a: Destination, plus 10 percent of trip time, plus alternate if required, plus 30 minutes holding at 1500 ft.
qOrig: What are the dispatch fuel requirements for Flag operations?
detail: Flag flights must be dispatched with enough fuel to fly to and land at the destination; then fly for 10 percent of the total time required to fly from the departure airport to and land at the destination; then fly to and land at the most distant alternate if one is required; then fly for 30 minutes at holding speed at 1500 ft above the destination airport, or the alternate if one is required.
quote: "Fly for 30 minutes at holding speed at 1500 ft above the destination airport"
note: 14 CFR 121.645. The 10 percent is of TOTAL trip time, which is what distinguishes Flag from the B043 special reserve where the 10 percent applies only to oceanic/remote continental time. Applicable areas at 8.1.1.2.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
q: Supplemental dispatch fuel requirement?
a: Not separately published at 8.3.2. The applicable Part 121 supplemental rule governs.
qOrig: What are the dispatch fuel requirements for Supplemental operations?
detail: FOM 8.3.2 publishes Domestic (8.3.2.1), Flag (8.3.2.2) and the Special Fuel Reserves in International Operations under B043 (8.3.2.3). Supplemental operations are referenced elsewhere in Chapter 8 and in 2.1.1, which makes clear the PIC and Dispatcher are jointly responsible for operating all domestic, flag and supplemental operations per the applicable regulations.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
q: B043 special fuel requirement?
a: Destination, 10 percent of oceanic time only, alternate if required, plus 45 minutes at normal cruise burn.
qOrig: What are the special fuel requirements for a B043 flight plan?
detail: Under Ops Spec B043 flights must be dispatched with enough fuel to fly to and land at the destination; then fly for 10 percent of the PLANNED TIME IN OCEANIC/REMOTE CONTINENTAL AIRSPACE; then fly to and land at the most distant alternate if one is required; then fly for 45 minutes at normal cruising consumption, calculated at the flight's weight and altitude at top of descent.
ref: FOM 8.3.2.3 Special Fuel Reserves in International Operations (737/787/A321/A330)
quote: "Fly for a period of 10% of the planned time in oceanic/remote continental airspace"
note: This is the key contrast with Flag: B043 applies the 10 percent only to oceanic/remote continental time, not the whole trip, and the final reserve is 45 minutes at normal cruise consumption rather than 30 minutes holding at 1500 ft. Explicitly banners 787. That is what makes B043 fuel-efficient on Pacific routes.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
q: What is final reserve fuel?
a: The last protected fuel. 30 minutes holding at 1500 ft for Flag, or 45 minutes at cruise burn under B043.
qOrig: What is Final Reserve Fuel?
detail: Final reserve is the fuel that must remain untouched at the end of the planned profile. For Flag operations it is 30 minutes at holding speed at 1500 ft above the destination or alternate. Under the B043 special international reserve it is 45 minutes at normal cruising consumption computed at the flight's weight and altitude at top of descent. For domestic it is 45 minutes at last cruise altitude consumption with an alternate, or 55 minutes with none.
quote: "Fly for 45 minutes at normal cruising consumption."
note: Tie this to 11.2.6: if it becomes apparent you will land with less than 30 minutes of fuel, declare MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY FUEL. Final reserve is a planning number; the 30-minute emergency-fuel trigger is an in-flight number.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
q: When do you ask ATC about the delay?
a: When an airborne delay plus a diversion could land you with less than 30 minutes of fuel.
qOrig: When should you plan to “inquire” from ATC the current delay situation when unanticipated
detail: The PIC should request ATC delay information if it is anticipated that an airborne delay followed by a diversion could result in landing with less than a 30-minute fuel supply. FOM 11.2.5 reinforces the same posture: crews should be proactive in assessing estimated arrival fuel and, if delays are anticipated that could lead to minimum fuel, should evaluate and inquire well in advance.
quote: "The PIC should request ATC delay information if it is anticipated that an airborne delay followed by a diversion could result in landing with less than a 30-minute fuel supply."
note: Inquire early. By the time you can declare minimum fuel you have already committed to an airport and given up the divert option.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
q: When do you declare minimum fuel?
a: Once committed to a specific airport and able to accept little or no delay.
qOrig: When should you declare Minimum Fuel?
detail: Minimum fuel means the fuel supply has reached a state where the flight can accept little or no delay. Declare it only after committing to land at a specific airport. Do not declare it at the destination while a divert to the alternate is still available. It is an advisory, not an emergency, and grants no priority.
quote: "should only be made when the flight has committed to land at a specific airport"
note: The FOM also directs crews to be proactive and inquire well in advance if delays could lead to minimum fuel.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
q: When do you declare MAYDAY FUEL?
a: When it becomes apparent you will land with less than 30 minutes of fuel.
qOrig: When should you declare “MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, FUEL”?
detail: The PIC shall declare MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY FUEL when it becomes apparent that landing will occur with less than a 30-minute supply of fuel, to ensure priority handling. The 30-minute supply is based on holding fuel flow or higher, as required by configuration, at 1500 ft above field elevation.
quote: "the PIC shall declare, “MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, FUEL” to ensure priority handling."
note: Note shall, not should. Thirty minutes is a floor, not a target. Contrast with 11.2.5 minimum fuel, which is advisory and grants no priority.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
group: Assess Diversion and Alternate Airport Weather Conditions and Minima
q: Airborne, what weather do you need at destination and alternates?
a: Crew operating minima. To begin the final approach segment, reported RVR or visibility at or above the approach minimums.
qOrig: Once airborne, what does the weather have to be at your destination, destination alternate, ETOPS
detail: In flight, alternates must be at or above the crew's operating minima and remain suitable to conduct an IAP. To START the approach, do not begin the final approach segment unless the latest reported RVR, visibility, or ceiling if required, is at or above the authorized minimums. If a below-minimums report arrives after the final approach segment has begun, you may continue to DA/DH or MDA.
quote: "Do not begin the final approach segment of an instrument approach procedure unless the latest reported RVR, visibility, or ceiling (if required) is at or above the authorized minimums."
note: Three different standards get confused here: dispatch planning minima (8.2.2.1), in-flight suitability (crew operating minima, 6.3.5), and the approach-start gate (5.6.11). Keep them separate in an oral.

qOrig: How can you get the most current METAR/TAF when in oceanic airspace?
detail: ACARS is the primary means of pulling current METAR and TAF in oceanic airspace, with SATCOM or HF contact with Dispatch as the alternative. FOM 6.3.5 makes clear that Dispatch monitors airports in the ETOPS area of operation and will inform the Flight Crew of significant changes at adequate airports and designated alternates.
ref: FOM 6.3.5 In-Flight ETOPS Alternate Airport Weather Requirements
quote: "Dispatch will inform the Flight Crew of significant changes at adequate airports and designated alternates."
note: DESKTOP: the specific ACARS weather-request menu path is aircraft/ACARS documentation. The obligation direction is worth noting for an oral: Dispatch pushes significant changes to you, you do not rely solely on pulling them.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)

q: How often do you check destination and alternate weather?
a: Often enough to keep the diversion decision live. Dispatch monitors in parallel and pushes changes.
qOrig: How often should you be checking the weather at your destination and alternates?
detail: The FOM frames this as joint PIC and Dispatcher responsibility rather than a fixed interval. Dispatch must evaluate weather, landing distances, airport services and facilities for the earliest to latest ETA at designated ETOPS alternates, will inform the crew of significant changes, will update alternates if conditions preclude safe approach and landing, and will provide a revised Flight Plan if alternates change.
ref: FOM 6.3.5 In-Flight ETOPS Alternate Airport Weather Requirements
quote: "Dispatch will update ETOPS alternates if any conditions preclude safe approach and landing at existing alternates."
note: No fixed interval is published. The practical standard is that you should never be surprised by destination or alternate weather at top of descent. Tie to the descent gouge: ATIS, Build, Bug, Brakes, Brief, RNP/Recall.

secTitle: Demonstrate Ability to Correctly Program Aircraft Guidance Systems Including Approach
q: What is SLOP for?
a: Mitigating collision risk and wake turbulence in oceanic airspace. It is standard practice.
qOrig: What is the purpose of SLOP?
detail: The Flight Crew should use SLOP as standard operating practice in normal oceanic operations to mitigate collision risk and wake turbulence. It addresses both wake vortex encounters and the heightened collision risk when non-normal events such as operational altitude deviation errors and turbulence-induced altitude deviations occur.
ref: FOM 5.7.4.7 Strategic Lateral Offsets in Oceanic Airspace
quote: "to mitigate collision risk and wake turbulence."
note: SLOP is generally accepted but disallowed in specific regions; check the AIP. Any aircraft overtaking another should offset within the procedure to create the least wake turbulence for the aircraft being overtaken.

secTitle: Demonstrate Ability to Correctly Program Aircraft Guidance Systems Including Approach
q: How far can you offset with SLOP?
a: Zero to 2.0 nm right of centerline, in 0.1 nm steps. Left is not authorized.
qOrig: Up to what distance/direction from the route is SLOP used/acceptable?
detail: SLOP is applied in relation to a route or track. The aircraft may fly zero, or up to a maximum of 2 nm right of course only, from 0.0 to 2.0 nm right of centerline in 0.1 nm increments. SLOP left of course is not authorized. The Captain may apply an offset outbound at the oceanic entry point but must return to centerline at the oceanic exit point.
ref: FOM 5.7.4.7 Strategic Lateral Offsets in Oceanic Airspace
quote: "SLOP left of course is not authorized."
note: Three legal positions in practice: centerline, 1 nm right, 2 nm right, though the FOM permits any 0.1 increment. No ATC clearance is needed. Must be back on centerline by the oceanic exit point.
