detail: FMC and CDU manipulation: alternate navigation, destination change, offset entry, wind uplink, descent initiation, and autopilot requirements on RNAV procedures. FCOM Chapter 11 and the FMS Pilot Guide. Related FOM policy: 5.7.4.7 SLOP for offsets and 5.7.4.8 Navigation Systems Failure.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: What weather do you need to begin an approach?
a: Reported RVR or visibility at or above the authorized minimums. Ceiling only where required.
qOrig: What must the Weather be in order to begin an approach? Ceiling and visibility?
detail: The reported weather at the destination must be at or above the visibility minimums prescribed for the approach. Do not begin the final approach segment unless the latest reported RVR, visibility, or ceiling if required, is at or above the authorized minimums. For non-precision and CAT I, TDZ RVR is controlling, Mid and Rollout are advisory, and Mid may substitute for TDZ if TDZ is unavailable.
quote: "TDZ RVR reports are controlling."
note: Visibility is the controlling parameter; ceiling applies only where the procedure requires it. RVR values above 6000 are advisory only. Visibility below 1/2 sm is not authorized and shall not be used for approach minimums.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: Lowest visibility for CAT I?
a: Standard CAT I is 1800 RVR. Reduced minima CAT I is at FOM 5.6.16.
qOrig: What is the lowest visibility for a CAT I approach?
detail: FOM 5.6.16 covers CAT I Reduced Precision CAT I Landing Minima, which is the mechanism for going below standard CAT I. The absolute floor across all approaches is set by 5.6.11: visibility below 1/2 sm is not authorized and shall not be used for approach minimums.
ref: FOM 5.6.16 CAT I Reduced Precision CAT I Landing Minima / 5.6.11

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: Are there high mins Captain restrictions?
a: Yes. Exemption 5549 relieves them. FOM 3.16.
qOrig: Are there restrictions for High Mins Captains?
detail: FOM 5.6.17 cross-references 3.16 Exemption 5549 for high minimums Captain limitations. A newly qualified Captain operates to increased minimums until the experience requirement is met, and Exemption 5549 is the FAA relief that modifies how those high-minimums restrictions apply.
quote: "See 3.16 – Exemption 5549 for high minimums Captain limitations."
note: DESKTOP: read FOM 3.16 for the exact hour threshold and the precise relief Exemption 5549 grants. This is directly relevant to you as a new Captain and is a near-certain oral question, so get the numbers from the PDF rather than from memory.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: What is FAA Exemption 5549?
a: The exemption governing high minimums Captain restrictions. FOM 3.16.
qOrig: What is FAA Exemption 5549?
detail: Exemption 5549 is the FAA exemption addressed at FOM 3.16 that governs the high minimums restriction applied to newly qualified Captains, cross-referenced from FOM 5.6.17 Category II/III Operational Requirements.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: Lowest visibility for CAT II?
a: Ops Spec C060. Read the value off the PRC approach briefing card.
qOrig: What is the lowest visibility for a CAT II approach? (C060)
detail: CAT II/III operational requirements are FOM 5.6.17 under Ops Spec C060, and the FOM explicitly directs that the approach briefing references and required equipment tables in the PRC/QRH contain the complete listings. The FOM does not duplicate the minima table.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: Lowest visibility for CAT II SA?
a: Ops Spec C060. The value is on the PRC approach briefing card.
qOrig: What is the lowest visibility for a CAT II SA approach? (C060)
detail: Same source as CAT II. FOM 5.6.17 defers to the PRC/QRH approach briefing references and required equipment tables. SA CAT II also carries the 5.6.17.2 gate: the final approach segment may not begin unless controlling RVR is at or above authorized minimums and the required airborne and ground equipment is operational.
ref: FOM 5.6.17.2 CAT II/SA CAT II Operating Limitations

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: Lowest visibility for CAT III?
a: Ops Spec C060. The value is on the PRC approach briefing card.
qOrig: What is the lowest visibility for a CAT III approach? (C060)
detail: FOM 5.6.17 defers CAT III minima to the PRC/QRH approach briefing references and required equipment tables. Autoland is the approved means on the 787 and is permitted on CAT II/III runways only, with the PIC required to be Autoland qualified.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: Does the FOM table CAT II and III limitations?
a: No. It points to the PRC and QRH tables instead.
qOrig: Is there a table in the FOM categorizing CAT II/III Approach and Landing Limitations?
detail: FOM 5.6.17 directs Flight Crews to use the approach procedures in the fleet-specific manuals for all CAT II/III approaches. The approach briefing references and required equipment tables in the PRC/QRH contain the complete listings of Flight Crew procedures and required equipment. Missed approach criteria for CAT II/III are also in the fleet-specific manuals.
quote: "The approach briefing references and required equipment tables in the PRC/QRH contain complete listings of the Flight Crew procedures and required equipment."
note: Ops Spec C060. Also: Alaska may be restricted by variant from CAT II/III at certain runway/airport combinations, see the tailored Jeppesen chart notes (5.6.17.1).

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: When can you autoland?
a: CAT II and III runways only. On the 787 the PIC must be Autoland qualified.
qOrig: Under what conditions can you perform an autoland?
detail: Autoland approaches and landings are permitted on CAT II/III runways ONLY. Pilots should advise the tower any time Autoland operations are conducted so the ILS Critical Zone is protected; that critical area is normally protected when weather is below 800 ft or 2 miles. On the 787 the PIC must be Autoland qualified. The procedures themselves are in the fleet-specific manuals.
quote: "Autoland approaches and landings are permitted on CAT II/III runways only."
note: Ops Spec C061. Two traps: it is a CAUTION-level restriction, and the tower advisory is on you because in good weather the ILS critical area is not automatically protected. Note the portal previously carried a wrong claim that the Hawaiian 787 cannot autoland on an ILS; the FCOM note is conditional on detected glideslope interference, not fleet-wide.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: When must you autoland?
a: Autoland is the approved means for CAT II and III. The 787 PIC must be qualified and have one automatic landing in the aircraft.
qOrig: Under what conditions must you perform an autoland?
detail: For CAT II/III, Autoland and (737) HGS AIII hand-flown approaches are approved. For HA the Captain must complete one automatic landing in the aircraft to be qualified for CAT II/III Autoland operations. On the 787 the PIC must be Autoland qualified per 5.6.18. Autoland is permitted on CAT II/III runways only.
quote: "(HA) The Captain must complete one automatic landing in the aircraft to be qualified for CAT II/III (Autoland) operations."
note: This is a currency item that bites new Captains: without that one automatic landing logged in the aircraft, you are not CAT II/III qualified regardless of sim performance. Autoland reporting requirements are at FOM 7.1.14.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: How do you log an autoland?
a: Record all Autoland and HGS AIII landings on the ACARS Flight Summary page.
qOrig: What are the requirements to log/report an autoland?
detail: Record all Autoland/HGS AIII landings on the ACARS Flight Summary page. For guidance on completing the A/C Approach Survey section of the Maintenance Logbook, HA crews use 5.6.21 Maintenance Request for Autoland.
quote: "Record all Autoland/HGS AIII landings on the ACARS Flight Summary page."
note: Two separate actions: the ACARS Flight Summary entry and the Maintenance Logbook A/C Approach Survey. As HA, 5.6.21 is your reference, not the AS reliability program at 5.6.20.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: What drives a diversion?
a: Anything degrading your ability to land safely at destination. An engine shutdown mandates the nearest suitable airport.
qOrig: What factors may precipitate a diversion?
detail: If an engine fails or is shut down in flight, land at the nearest suitable airport based on time considerations where a safe landing can be made. Suitability factors include aircraft configuration, weight, systems status and fuel remaining, and wind and weather conditions enroute at the diversion altitude. As soon as possible after a shutdown the Captain shall notify ATC and Dispatch and continue to provide timely progress information, and a safety report shall be completed.
ref: FOM 11.2.7 / 11.2.7.1 Engine Shutdown in Flight, Nearest Suitable Airport
quote: "land the aircraft at the nearest suitable airport, based on time considerations, where a safe landing can be made."
note: Nearest Suitable Airport is FAA-approval-required text, so it is regulatory, not company preference. Nothing justifies flying past the nearest suitable airport after an engine shutdown.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: When do you start the divert?
a: Fuel against final reserve, weather trend, field condition, configuration and systems, and the joint PIC and Dispatcher call.
qOrig: What factors should you consider when deciding when to start diverting to your alternate?
detail: Build the decision from the fuel rules and the suitability factors. Minimum fuel should only be declared once committed to a specific airport and not while a divert is still available (11.2.5), so the divert decision must be made before that point. Suitability factors from 11.2.7.1 are aircraft configuration, weight, systems status and fuel remaining, and wind and weather conditions enroute at the diversion altitude. Dispatch and the PIC exercise judgment jointly on the safest course of action.
quote: "it should not be made at the destination when the decision to divert to an alternate is still available."
note: That quote is the timing test. If you are still holding at destination with the alternate available, you are not in minimum fuel yet, and that is exactly the window in which the divert decision belongs. Waiting until you can declare minimum fuel means you waited too long.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: Not using your listed alternate. What do you weigh?
a: Nearest suitable airport factors: configuration, weight, systems, fuel, and enroute wind and weather at diversion altitude.
qOrig: If you are not diverting to your listed alternate, what factors should you consider before selecting the
detail: Suitability factors listed in the FOM include aircraft configuration, weight, systems status and fuel remaining, and wind and weather conditions enroute at the diversion altitude. The list is explicitly non-exhaustive. After an engine shutdown you must land at the nearest suitable airport based on time considerations where a safe landing can be made.
quote: "The following factors and others may be relevant in determining whether or not an airport is suitable"
note: Nearest Suitable Airport is FAA-approval-required text. Note it says nearest suitable based on TIME, not distance. DESKTOP: read the full factor list off 11.2.7.1, I captured only the first two bullets this session.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: Where is fuel planning in the FOM?
a: FOM 8.3. Planning factors at 8.3.1.1, requirements at 8.3.2.
qOrig: Where in the FOM is the fuel planning section?
detail: Section 8.3 carries fuel: 8.3.1 Fuel Planning, 8.3.1.1 Fuel Planning Factors, 8.3.1.2 Departure Fuel Coordination, 8.3.1.3 Tanker Fuel, 8.3.2 Fuel Requirements with 8.3.2.1 Domestic, 8.3.2.2 Flag and 8.3.2.3 Special Fuel Reserves in International Operations. In-flight fuel emergencies are separate, at 11.2.5 Minimum Fuel and 11.2.6 Emergency Fuel.
quote: "No flight may begin its takeoff roll with less than (AS) REQ Fuel and (HA) MIN TAKEOFF FUEL."
note: Tanker fuel labels are worth knowing: economic tankering shows as (HA) EXTRA, mandatory tankering as (HA) CONT.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: What is the ETOPS critical fuel scenario?
a: Fuel to fly from the most critical point to an ETOPS alternate assuming a specified failure. It must be covered at dispatch.
qOrig: What is the ETOPS Critical Fuel Scenario?
detail: Critical fuel is computed for the most limiting diversion on the route, assuming the critical failure case, and compared against planned fuel at that point. If planned fuel is less than critical fuel, the release requires additional fuel.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: What is LAHSO?
a: Land and Hold Short Operations. Landing and stopping short of a hold short point on the runway.
qOrig: What is LAHSO?
detail: LAHSO involves landing and holding short of an intersecting runway, an intersecting taxiway, or some other designated point on a runway. The Available Landing Distance (ALD) is measured from the landing threshold to the hold short point, and the hold short point is marked by a painted holding position marking and red and white hold short position signs.
quote: "A point on the runway beyond which a landing aircraft with a LAHSO clearance is not authorized to proceed."
note: Revisions to this section require FAA approval, which signals it is regulatory text, not company preference.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: What must you check before accepting LAHSO?
a: The Captain accepts only if all published conditions are met, and must confirm stopping within the ALD using AFM distance plus 1000 ft.
qOrig: What are the 4 different factors that must be considered prior to accepting a LAHSO clearance?
detail: The Captain may accept a LAHSO clearance only if every condition in 5.6.32.2 is satisfied. The HA determination is that existing conditions allow the aircraft to safely land and stop within the Available Landing Distance, where calculated landing distance equals the FAA-approved AFM distance plus 1000 ft for the actual configuration, environment and weight.
quote: "The calculated landing distance will be the FAA-approved Aircraft Flight Manual (AFM) distance plus 1000 ft"
note: RECONCILE: Rev 125 revised LAHSO guidance to prohibit LAHSO on wet runways and require tailwind to be calm, less than 3 kts. Confirm the current four-factor list against the Rev 125.1 PDF before quoting it on the line. The AS note also requires a published 10-7 LAHSO page for that airport and runway configuration.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: What is a TLR?
a: Takeoff and Landing Report. The performance analysis for a specific runway and conditions.
qOrig: What is a TLR?
detail: The TLR is the performance product used for runway analysis. FOM 5.6.22.1 sets the surrounding policy: Captains shall ensure landing is allowed and executed within the appropriate performance data, and the landing data used for in-flight analysis is based on input conditions, which is what makes an accurate runway assessment critical.
quote: "The landing data used for in-flight analysis is based on input conditions, this highlights the importance of an accurate runway assessment."
note: Acceptance is not weight-only: environmental conditions matter equally. Do not interchange the takeoff and landing crosswind tables, they serve different functions and the takeoff table is CG and weight sensitive while the TALPA landing table is not.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: How do you request landing performance data?
a: Load closeout, TPR and TLR. FOM 5.2 and fleet performance.
qOrig: How can you request landing data performance?
detail: Load closeout reading and verification, and the takeoff/landing performance products. Takeoff performance hierarchy is Final TPR, then Preliminary TPR, then TLR. Using a TLR for takeoff demands attention to the temperature and altimeter assumptions baked into it. FOM 5.2 covers closeout and weight and balance; the SABLE Load Sheet is the official FAA weight and balance record. Landing analysis designators and request methods are in the performance system documentation.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: What do HXX/TXX and LXX/RXX mean on the printout?
a: Load closeout, TPR and TLR. FOM 5.2 and fleet performance.
qOrig: On the landing data analysis printout, what do the designator/s “HXX/TXX” and “LXX/RXX” represent?
detail: Load closeout reading and verification, and the takeoff/landing performance products. Takeoff performance hierarchy is Final TPR, then Preliminary TPR, then TLR. Using a TLR for takeoff demands attention to the temperature and altimeter assumptions baked into it. FOM 5.2 covers closeout and weight and balance; the SABLE Load Sheet is the official FAA weight and balance record. Landing analysis designators and request methods are in the performance system documentation.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival

q: What is in the arrival and approach TPC briefing?
a: Threats from PM and PF, Plan from PF, Considerations from PF. The PF starts it before descent.
qOrig: What items compose the Arrival and Approach TPC Briefing?
detail: Prior to beginning the descent the PF initiates the approach briefing, which should be interactive, concise and focused on the big picture. T, Threats, shared: the PM identifies relevant threats using the threat list on the Crew Briefing Reference Card and any airport-specific threats in the 10-7, and the PF briefs additional threats as needed. P, Plan, PF: route including STAR, approach and approach mode; relevant altitude and airspeed constraints and approach minimums; fuel and route to alternate; missed approach; landing runway, assessment, exit and taxi; autobrakes; flaps and approach speed. C, Considerations, PF: specific PM duties based on threats and plan, any other issues, and a recap of critical threats as desired.
quote: "Pilots jointly identify any relevant threats, followed by the PF presenting the arrival plan"
note: Threats is the only shared element; Plan and Considerations are PF. Management strategies are discussed as threats are identified rather than saved to the end. The departure equivalent is briefed the same way, see FOM 1.3.1 in the workbook.

q: Inside the FAF. Minimum visibility?
a: You may not begin the final approach segment below minimums. Once begun, continue to DA or MDA.
qOrig: What if you are inside the FAF? Minimum visibility?
detail: For CAT II and SA CAT II, the Final Approach Segment may not begin unless the latest controlling RVR reports for the landing runway are at or above the authorized minimums AND the required airborne equipment is operational AND the ground equipment is operational: localizer and glide slope, an outer marker or DME defining the FAF (a published waypoint or minimum GS intercept altitude fix may substitute), and High Intensity Runway Lights or foreign equivalent. If a below-minimums report arrives after the final approach segment has begun, you may continue to DA/DH or MDA per 5.6.11.

quote: "The Final Approach Segment (FAS) of an IAP may not begin unless the latest controlling RVR reports for the landing runway are at or above the minimums authorized"
note: Note visibility below 1/2 sm is not authorized and shall not be used for approach minimums (5.6.11).

q: Factored vs unfactored landing data?
a: Unfactored is raw demonstrated distance. Factored adds margin, and the 787 model adds 15 percent including air distance.
qOrig: What is the difference between factored vs unfactored landing data?
detail: Unfactored landing distance is the raw computed distance. Factored distance applies a safety margin on top. Rev 125 moved the 787 to a TALPA landing model using a 7-second air/flare distance and a 15 percent margin on TOTAL landing distance including air distance, calculated to a computed rather than fixed touchdown point. The 737 LTP calculation shows the same principle: minimum landing distance includes air-run to touchdown plus ground roll plus a 15 percent safety factor for degraded braking action.
quote: "this distance includes air-run to touchdown plus ground roll and a 15% safety factor for degraded braking action requests"
note: DESKTOP: read 5.6.22.3 in full for the 787-specific wording, since Rev 125 removed HA bannering there and added fleet-specific guidance. The quoted 15 percent text above is from the 737 LTP paragraph, so do not attribute it to the 787 model without checking.

q: When is an HF position report required?
a: When you are not on CPDLC. Under CPDLC you do not make HF position reports.
qOrig: When is an HF position report required?
detail: Flight Crews should NOT make HF position reports when using CPDLC procedures. When using CPDLC you must contact ARINC after a successful CPDLC logon but prior to the initial Gateway Fix to obtain a SELCAL check on HF, establishing a backup if CPDLC fails. No other HF reports need be made while using CPDLC. Non-CPDLC position reporting varies by area and is specified on the enroute chart.
quote: "Flight Crews should not make HF position reports when using CPDLC procedures."
note: REV 125.1 ADDED: if SELCAL is not functioning, one member of the crew must listen to HF continuously. That is the new sentence in this revision and a likely oral question. Non-CPDLC reporting is 5.7.3.19; for the Oakland FIR the procedures are in FD Pro X under Pubs, Pacific, Oceanic Position Reporting Procedures.

secTitle: Demonstrate Dangerous Goods Policies and Procedures
q: How do you fight a lithium battery fire?
a: HALON first, then cool the device with water. Never use ice.
qOrig: How do you fight a lithium battery fire?
detail: FIGHT THE FIRE with a HALON extinguisher. Water may be used to fight a lithium ION battery fire but should NOT be used on a lithium METAL battery fire. It is very important to prevent the fire spreading to adjacent flammable materials. Then COOL THE DEVICE using water preferably, or any non-alcoholic liquid if water is not available (milk, fruit juice, POG). AVOID USING ICE, which acts as an insulator; if the device is insulated before it is fully cooled, remaining cells that have not reached thermal runaway could ignite. If the fire is on the Flight Deck the device must immediately be removed by any means available (gloves, blanket).
ref: FOM 11.1.10.2 PED Fire Containment Bag (Yellow Bag)
quote: "AVOID USING ICE to cool the device. Ice will act as an insulator."
note: It may take 15 or more minutes to completely cool the device. REV 125.1: this is the YELLOW bag section, renumbered from 11.1.10. The new RED bag procedure at 11.1.10.1 is a containment procedure, not a firefighting one: gloves, device into the bag, pull the red tab, seal the Velcro, zip, and place it outside the Flight Deck Door. HA aircraft switch yellow to red from October 1.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Where are the US holding speeds?
a: FOM 5.5.15 Holding, US Holding Speed and Time table.
qOrig: Where can you find the holding speeds (FAR) in USA?
detail: US holding speeds: 6000 ft or below, 200 KIAS. Above 6000 through 14,000 ft, 230 KIAS (or 210 KIAS where restricted), inbound leg 1 minute. Above 14,000 ft, 265 KIAS, inbound leg 1 1/2 minutes. Standard holding patterns are right-hand turns. Begin speed reduction no earlier than three minutes prior to the fix.
quote: "Standard holding patterns are right-hand turns."
note: Holding pattern protection is based on a maximum of 280 KIAS or Mach 0.8, whichever is lower. Civil aircraft at military or joint airports should expect max 230 KIAS. Alaska and New York are restricted to 210 KIAS above 6000 through 14,000 ft where charts show the standard holding symbol with 210K in the center; in Alaska that does not apply in the Anchorage or Fairbanks approach control areas. Advise ATC if a higher speed is needed for turbulence, icing or configuration.
